# Sources: history, topic discovery

Ledger for the topic-discovery stage of a ten-minute narrated history video. Chosen subject: the Mountains of Kong (T1).
Alternatives researched lightly: the Blanc telegraph fraud (T2) and the Vasa (T3). Each `- Access:` line says how much
of the source was actually read: read (the page itself was opened and read), indirect (only through another source),
snippet (only a search summary: a lead, never a source). Pages were read through a page-reading tool that answers from
the page and quotes only short passages; where that limited the reading, the entry says so.

### S1. Thomas J. Bassett and Philip W. Porter, "'From the Best Authorities': The Mountains of Kong in the Cartography of West Africa", The Journal of African History 32 (3): 367-413, Cambridge University Press, November 1991 (online 22 January 2009)
- Primary for its own survey of the maps (the composite of forty maps naming the range, with their lengths and latitudes, is the study's data); secondary, peer-reviewed scholarship for the history of Rennell, Park and Binger. Authors at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign and the University of Minnesota. DOI 10.1017/S0021853700031522. URL: https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-african-history/article/from-the-best-authorities-the-mountains-of-kong-in-the-cartography-of-west-africa/25D7E0376A0889142FFA6DF737285E98
- Access: read (the Cambridge Core page: abstract, footnotes and references; the tool paraphrased the abstract and quoted the footnotes; the article body was behind an access wall and was not read)
- Supports: C01, C02, C03, C04, C07, C08, C09, C10, C11, C15, C16, C17. Counterevidence: none on the finding. Popular pages give "several hundred" maps (C20, unverified) against this study's forty, but the forty is a composite the authors gathered, not a census. An explorer's 2017 book says the mountains exist (S8, C21); no scholarly support for it turned up.
- Status: the standard study of the subject. No newer scholarship replacing it turned up in this stage's searches, which were not exhaustive. Check the footnote figures (C10) against the article itself before a script states them.

### S2. Amelia Raines, "Improvements in Geography: An 18th-Century Map of North Africa", Library of Congress, Geography and Map Division blog, 7 April 2023
- Secondary (institutional), describing a primary record in the Library's collection: Rennell's 1798 map. URL: https://blogs.loc.gov/maps/2023/04/improvements-in-geography-an-18th-century-map-of-north-africa/
- Access: read (the whole post)
- Supports: C01, C03, C05, C06, C12, C13. Counterevidence: none. The post does not say who disproved the range or when, or how long it stayed on maps.
- Status: credible institutional account written from the map itself, so it is independent of S1. It agrees with S1 on the 1798 map and on the range not existing ("there are no Mountains of Kong").

### S3. Princeton University Library (Rare Books Division), "Lander Brothers", undated page on the Library's Africa maps website, describing Richard and John Lander, Journal of an Expedition to Explore the Course and Termination of the Niger (London: John Murray, 1832, 3 vols)
- Secondary (institutional description of a primary record, the Landers' published journal). URL: https://static-prod.lib.princeton.edu/visual_materials/maps/websites/africa/lander/lander.html
- Access: read (the whole page)
- Supports: C12, C14. Counterevidence: popular summaries (Wikipedia, seen as snippets) differ on secondary dates (arrival at Bussa, start of the float) but agree on the 1830 voyage to the sea.
- Status: credible, and the only read source on the 1830 voyage, because the Britannica page refused the request (HTTP 403). The page names no institution or date itself; the attribution comes from its URL and its Rare Books Division reference.

### S4. Wikipedia, "Mountains of Kong", encyclopedia article (revision not seen)
- Popular (encyclopedia). URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountains_of_Kong
- Access: snippet (search summaries only; the page was not opened)
- Supports, as leads only: C02, C18, C19. Counterevidence: none seen.
- Status: lead only. The summaries show it repeating S1's count, so it is not independent of S1.

### S5. Big Think, article on the Mountains of Kong (Strange Maps column; author and date not seen)
- Popular (magazine website). URL: https://bigthink.com/?p=52052
- Access: snippet
- Supports, as a lead: C19 (a last appearance in Trampler's Mittelschulatlas, Vienna, 1905). The search summary did not say which result gave the 1905 atlas; this page and S4 were among them.
- Status: lead only.

### S6. Mental Floss, "The Mountains of Kong: The Majestic West African Range That Never Existed" (author and date not seen)
- Popular (magazine website). URL: https://www.mentalfloss.com/geography/maps/mountains-kong-majestic-west-african-range-never-existed
- Access: snippet
- Supports, as leads: C18 (Binger at the town of Kong on 20 February 1888) and C20 ("several hundred" maps); which result gave which line was not shown. The same search turned up the line "mosques instead of mountains", which was dropped under the content rules (notes.md).
- Status: lead only.

### S7. Altea Gallery (antique map dealer), "The first appearance of the infamous 'Mountains of Kong'", catalogue listing for Rennell's 1798 map
- Popular (a commercial description of a primary record offered for sale). URL: https://alteagallery.com/products/africa/north-africa/north-africa-maps-north-africa/the-first-appearance-of-the-infamous-mountains-of-kong/
- Access: snippet (title in the search listing only)
- Supports, as a lead: C02.
- Status: lead only.

### S8. Julian Monroe Fisher, Mountains of Kong (book, 2017), as reported by InsideHook, "Did a Real-Life Indiana Jones Just Find the Long-Lost Mountains of Kong?"
- Popular (an explorer's travel book, reported by a lifestyle website). URL: https://www.insidehook.com/books/book-on-fabled-mountains-kong-africa-julian-monroe-fisher
- Access: snippet
- Supports: C21 (the claim that the mountains exist). Counterevidence: S1 and S2; no peer-reviewed or independent support found.
- Status: unverified popular counter-claim. Recorded so the ledger shows the disagreement; not used.

### S9. Randy H. Katz, "Napoleon's Secret Weapon", lecture notes for course CS39C, University of California, Berkeley, last updated 14 February 1997
- Secondary (a university teaching outline that names no sources). URL: https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~randy/Courses/CS39C.S97/optical/optical.html
- Access: read (the whole page)
- Supports: C22, C23, C24. Counterevidence: the page gives 1836 and names nobody; popular accounts give 1834 or 1836 and differ on a name and on the verdict (C25, C26).
- Status: the only credible page read on the fraud, and an outline rather than a publication. Gerard Holzmann and Björn Pehrson, The Early History of Data Networks (1994), is the likely fuller account; it was seen only in search listings and not read.

### S10. Amusing Planet, "The World's First Cyber Attack Happened Nearly Two Hundred Years Ago", March 2019
- Popular (website). URL: https://www.amusingplanet.com/2019/03/the-worlds-first-cyber-attack-happened.html
- Access: snippet
- Supports, as leads: C24, C25 (an 1834 start), C26 (released because no clear law covered misuse of the telegraph).
- Status: lead only.

### S11. Jim Cofer, "the first telecom scam", blog post, 14 November 2025
- Popular (blog). URL: https://jimcofer.com/2025/11/14/the-first-telecom-scam
- Access: snippet
- Supports, as leads: C24, C25, C26 (only the bribery could be charged; a law then made hijacking the telegraph a crime and banned private rival systems).
- Status: lead only. Disagrees with S10 on the verdict.

### S12. Parisian Fields, "The Rise and Fall of the Visual Telegraph", blog post, 5 November 2017
- Popular (blog). URL: https://parisianfields.com/2017/11/05/the-rise-and-fall-of-the-visual-telegraph/
- Access: snippet
- Supports, as a lead: C25 (names the brothers as François and Louis, not Joseph).
- Status: lead only. Disagrees with S10 and S11 on a name.

### S13. History of Information, "The Optical Telegraph: Faster than a Messenger on Horseback", quoting Holzmann and Pehrson (1994)
- Popular (reference website quoting a scholarly book). URL: https://www.historyofinformation.com/detail.php?entryid=496
- Access: snippet
- Supports, as a lead: C22 (556 stations over 4,800 km).
- Status: lead only. Agrees with S9 on the 556 stations.

### S14. Vasa Museum (Swedish National Maritime, Transport and Military Museums), "The Disaster", vasamuseet.se, last updated "7/2/2021" (as shown)
- Secondary (institutional: the museum that holds and studies the ship). URL: https://www.vasamuseet.se/en/vasa-history/disaster
- Access: read (the whole page)
- Supports: C27, C28, C29. Counterevidence: a popular page in the search gave 53 dead against this page's 30. The page does not describe the stability test, the inquest or the salvage.
- Status: credible. The one read source for this alternative.

### S15. Discover Magazine, "The Vasa Warship Sank After Only 25 Minutes of Sailing, Taking 30 Lives With it" (date not seen)
- Popular (magazine website). URL: https://www.discovermagazine.com/the-vasa-warship-sank-after-only-25-minutes-of-sailing-taking-30-lives-with-47131
- Access: snippet
- Supports, as leads: C27 (30 lives), C30 (the stability test; the summary did not say which result described it).
- Status: lead only.

### S16. Archaeology magazine (Archaeological Institute of America), Vasa feature, issue 1207 according to its URL
- Popular (magazine). URL: https://archive.archaeology.org/1207/features/vasa_warship_sweden_stockholm_harbor.html
- Access: snippet
- Supports, as leads: C30; the archaeologist Fred Hocker's view that the ship was top-heavy.
